title: Armenia Signs Big Deal with the U.S.—But Russia Isn't Happy
summary: Armenia just made a big move—it signed a new partnership with the United States! But this might upset its old friend, Russia. On Tuesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Armenia's Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan signed the deal in Yerevan, Armenia's capital. A key part is a 27-mile transportation corridor called the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP). It will go through southern Armenia, giving Azerbaijan a direct path to its exclave Nakhchivan and then to Turkey. The U.S. will own 74% of the company that builds it. Armenia's Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has been getting closer to the U.S. and Europe. That made Russia angry. Russia is Armenia's longtime ally, but it didn't help when Azerbaijan attacked the Nagorno-Karabakh region in 2023. Now, Russia warns it might raise the price of gas it sells to Armenia if the country keeps moving toward the West. Armenia has elections coming up in June, and some pro-Russia parties are challenging Pashinyan. The U.S. says this deal is about making money and peace together. "We are laying the groundwork for the sort of economic engagement that allows Armenians to make money and find prosperity and Americans to do the same," Rubio said. It's a tricky balance for Armenia—new friends in the West, but an old ally watching closely.
why_it_matters: This story shows how countries sometimes have to make tough choices between old allies and new opportunities—and how those choices can affect everyday things like the price of gas and the stability of a whole region.

background_read: Armenia is a small country in the South Caucasus region that used to be part of the Soviet Union. It has been locked in a long conflict with neighboring Azerbaijan over the Nagorno‑Karabakh region, where fighting erupted again in 2023.
Russia, a longtime ally, angered many Armenians by not stepping in during that war, pushing Armenia to seek closer ties with the West.
The new U.S. deal includes a corridor through southern Armenia that would connect Azerbaijan’s exclave Nakhchivan to the rest of Azerbaijan and then to Turkey.
Article_Structure: WHO: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Armenia’s Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, and Russia.
WHAT: Armenia signed a partnership with the U.S., including a corridor project called TRIPP that links Azerbaijan’s exclave Nakhchivan to the country, while Russia threatens to raise gas prices.
WHERE: Yerevan, Armenia’s capital; the corridor runs through southern Armenia.
WHY: Armenia seeks economic growth and closer Western ties after being disappointed by Russia’s inaction during the 2023 Nagorno‑Karabakh conflict.

perspectives.description: Armenian leaders believe the deal could boost the economy and bring new jobs through the corridor and U.S. investment.
Russia sees the partnership as a betrayal and may cut off cheap gas or support pro‑Russia politicians to weaken the Armenian government.
Some international observers view this as a normal geopolitical shift, where smaller countries try to balance between big powers to survive.
